item.title: Supreme Court Allows Trump Plan to Restrict Mail-In Voting, for Now
item.description: The administration asked the court to clear the way for President Trump’s order that creates “state citizenship lists” and directs the Postal Service to decide who gets a mail-in ballot.
item.dc:creator: Abbie VanSickle and Ann E. Marimow
item.media:credit: Nick Hagen for The New York Times
item.media:description: Volunteers processing mail-in ballots on Nov. 5, 2024, in Dearborn, Mich.

item.title: Trump Has Quietly Sought Control Over Postal Service to Transform U.S. Elections
item.description: That effort got new attention on Monday, when the Supreme Court allowed preparations for mail voting curbs to proceed. The justices said it is not a final determination on the order’s legality.
item.dc:creator: Zolan Kanno-Youngs, Adam Sella and Nick Corasaniti
item.media:credit: Mario Tama/Getty Images
item.media:description: President Trump and his allies are trying to transform the U.S. Postal Service into a key player in their efforts to transform the nation’s elections.

item.title: Justices Allow Plans to Restrict Mail Voting, for Now
item.description: Also, the college admissions process is shifting once again. Here’s the latest at the end of Monday.

item.title: Trump Lays It on the Line for Darline Graham Ahead of South Carolina Runoff
item.description: The president rallied for the sister of Lindsey Graham in her South Carolina Senate run and pressured allies to endorse her. A super PAC run by his advisers has spent nearly $800,000 on her campaign. Will it be enough?
item.dc:creator: Emily Davies, Patricia Mazzei and Michael Gold
item.media:credit: Alex Kent/The New York Times
item.media:description: President Trump rallied for Senator Darline Graham of South Carolina in Myrtle Beach, S.C., on Friday, part of a full-court press to secure her victory in a special runoff primary Tuesday to replace her late brother.

item.title: With Trump Against Him, Can Ralph Norman Win in South Carolina?
item.description: The ultraconservative congressman who has broken with the president on spending is hoping voters reward his experience, contrarian streak and all.
item.dc:creator: Michael Gold
item.media:credit: Will Crooks for The New York Times
item.media:description: Representative Ralph Norman’s recalcitrant posture may have widened the rift that cleared the way for President Trump’s endorsement of Senator Darline Graham.

item.title: Can Democrats Win Back the Senate? Why Their Chances Are Improving.
item.description: Republicans still have some clear advantages on the map, but President Trump’s unpopularity has opened the door for an outcome that once seemed far-fetched.
item.dc:creator: Tim Balk
item.media:credit: Christopher Lee for The New York Times
item.media:description: James Talarico, a Democrat, is trying win a Senate race in Texas after decades of disappointments for his party.

item.title: Eon Huntley, the Democratic Socialist Running for Office While Working at Bergdorf
item.description: For Eon Huntley, who won his primary in New York in June, good clothes and populist policies go together.
item.dc:creator: Sandra E. Garcia
item.media:credit: James Estrin/The New York Times
item.media:description: Eon Huntley, a 41-year-old candidate for New York State Assembly, has juggled his full-time job at the luxury department store with running a Democratic Socialists of America-endorsed campaign.

item.title: Iran Pledges to Defy Trump’s Economic Sanctions
item.description: Analysts say Tehran could intensify the dispute militarily after the United States announced new efforts to squeeze Iran’s economy. One Iranian official vowed that “not a single drop of oil” would leave the gulf.
item.dc:creator: Aaron Boxerman, Sanam Mahoozi and Ephrat Livni
item.category: US and Israeli Attack on Iran (2026)
item.media:credit: Agence France-Presse — Getty Images
item.media:description: Motorists drive past an anti-American billboard in Tehran on Monday. President Trump has threatened Iran with “economic warfare and isolation on an unprecedented scale.”

item.title: Trump Threatens New 50% Tariffs on Cars, Trucks and Steel as U.S.-Canada Trade War Unfolds
item.description: President Trump vowed to increase tariffs on cars, trucks, auto parts and steel to 50 percent starting Jan. 1, as the countries edged toward a full-blown trade war.
item.dc:creator: Ana Swanson and Tony Romm
item.media:credit: Carlos Osorio/Reuters
item.media:description: Trade tensions between the United States and Canada have spiraled over the past few days, after the two sides failed to reach a trade deal and President Trump imposed 50 percent tariffs on $20 billion of the country’s exports on Saturday.

item.title: What’s Behind the U.S. Treasury’s Latest Attempt to Lower Interest Rates
item.description: The Treasury Department said it could begin to buy back more of its debt, and bond market investors are assessing the potential effects on borrowing costs.
item.dc:creator: Joe Rennison
item.media:credit: Kenny Holston/The New York Times

item.title: The Tour Guide Who Lived Through 9/11
item.description: Christina Stanton offers a very specific and deeply personal tour of the World Trade Center site to remind visitors what happened 25 years ago.
item.dc:creator: Michael Wilson
item.media:credit: James Estrin/The New York Times
item.media:description: Christina Stanton leads a North Carolina church youth group on a tour at the 9/11 Memorial reflecting pools. She carries a scrapbook of photos, including those of friends who died on 9/11.

item.title: What You Should Know About College Admissions Changes
item.description: After loosening requirements during the Covid era, some schools are shaking up admissions again, facing pressure from the Trump administration, A.I. and even their own professors.
item.dc:creator: Alan Blinder and Mark Arsenault
item.media:credit: Kendrick Brinson for The New York Times
item.media:description: Can you use A.I. to apply to college? Will the school ask for your test scores? Some schools are changing their policies.

item.title: Gov. Kathy Hochul, Five Years In, Makes Her Case for Four More
item.description: Ms. Hochul, who ascended to the governorship in the depths of the pandemic, believes that New York is back. She hopes she has persuaded New Yorkers.
item.dc:creator: Grace Ashford
item.media:credit: Amir Hamja for The New York Times
item.media:description: In five years of negotiating with state legislators, presidents and mayors, Gov. Kathy Hochul of New York has developed a distinctive political style.

item.title: The Mayor Went on Vacation. He Didn’t Travel Very Far.
item.description: Zohran Mamdani is known for working around the clock as mayor of New York City, but last week he and his wife headed “upstate” for vacation and some locals were thrilled to spot them.
item.dc:creator: Emma Goldberg
item.media:credit: Amir Hamja for The New York Times
item.media:description: Zohran Mamdani and Rama Duwaji, shown casting their votes for mayor last year, recently took a vacation in the Hudson Valley.

item.title: Opponents Sue to Stop Mamdani’s City-Owned Grocery Store Plan
item.description: A business group filed a lawsuit to stop New York City’s plan to open the five grocery stores, a campaign promise of Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s, arguing that it would hurt smaller stores.
item.dc:creator: Emma G. Fitzsimmons
item.media:credit: Heather Khalifa for The New York Times
item.media:description: The Multicultural Business Coalition represents the owners of some smaller stores that it says could be hurt by the city-owned grocery stores proposed by Mayor Zohran Mamdani.
